title: Why so many names
hook: a thousand names say that no single name can hold Him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaap for courage, and your line, borrow the courage. Did a line or a song walk you into something hard? Today, a step back to look at the whole hymn and ask a simple question. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

How many names do you have? Probably more than you think. Your full name on forms. A shorter one for friends. Something only your grandmother called you. Mom, or Dad, or Auntie, to someone. Babe, to someone else. A nickname from a soccer team that you'd rather forget. Each one is true. Each one holds a different piece of you. And not one of them, on its own, is the whole person. Now imagine trying to name someone infinitely larger than you. Today: why so many names.
screen: `A NAME ON FORMS, A NAME FOR FRIENDS.` → `WHAT YOUR GRANDMOTHER CALLED YOU.` → `NO ONE NAME IS THE WHOLE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Over the last four weeks you've heard a tiny slice of Jaap's names. Timeless. Merciful. Formless. Unborn. The armed One. Sun of suns. Lamp of beauty. Provider. Gobind. Home of compassion. Fearless. And there are hundreds more you haven't heard yet. Why so many? Jaap answered it in its first stanza: who can tell all Your names? Nobody. The wise speak the names drawn from Your deeds. So the long list isn't trying to finish the job. It's admitting the job can't be finished, and praising anyway. Each name is a window into one room of a house too big to see all at once. Guru Nanak said the same in Japji. In the nineteenth pauri, he says: countless are Your names, countless Your places. And then, with a smile you can almost hear, he adds that even the word countless is too heavy to carry. Notice too where the names come from. The Guru Granth Sahib calls the One by names from many places: Ram and Hari and Gobind, which Hindus also use; Allah and Khuda and Rahim, which Muslims also use; and the name that became the Sikh word of wonder, Waheguru. Jaap adds Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic names of its own. Sikhs don't treat any one of these as the password. The One, Sikh teaching holds, is beyond them all, and present in each. That's why the carry is more names than stars. Not because anyone has counted. Because, like the stars, the more you look, the more there are.
screen: `HUNDREDS OF NAMES IN ONE HYMN.` · `NO LIST CAN FINISH THE JOB.` · `JAPJI 19: COUNTLESS ARE YOUR NAMES.` · `NAMES FROM MANY LANGUAGES.` · then, large: `MORE NAMES THAN STARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write three names for the Divine. Grab a pen or open a note. Write three names. They can be ones you've learned here, like Akal or Kripaal, ones from your own background, or deed-names from your own life, like the one who carried me last winter. If the word Divine doesn't fit you, write three names for whatever you feel grateful toward. Read them slowly. Notice that each one opens a different window. Then sit with all three. The bell holds the time.
Why so many names. Because no single name can hold the One: Jaap's hundreds of names admit the list can never be finished, and praise anyway.
Your line: more names than stars. Tonight, if you can see the sky, look up and count a few stars, and let each one stand for one more name. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs call the One by many names in prayer and kirtan, Waheguru, Akal Purakh, Ram, Hari, Gobind, Kartar and more, following the Guru Granth Sahib, which uses names from many languages.

original.note: Gurmukhi: asankh naav, countless names, from Japji's nineteenth pauri.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jaap is long because it lists everything.
what it means: its hundreds of names admit that no single name can hold the One, and praise anyway.
what a scholar hears: Jaap's sahasranama-like form parallels Japji 19's 'asankh naav asankh thaav'; Gurbani draws divine names from Indic and Perso-Arabic usage alike.
